name: Sam Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at the big open-pit copper mine outside town, a Cat 793 that carries about two hundred and twenty tonnes a load. Start's at six, pre-start check on the truck, then it's loop after loop from the shovel down in the pit up to the crusher, twelve hours with a break at the crib room. I like the rhythm of it and I like the people, Rudy and I have eaten lunch together for nineteen years. What wears me out is the night roster now, my back doesn't forgive the cab seat like it used to.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You've been there nineteen years. How do you feel about the place?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's been good to me, I won't pretend otherwise, the union got us decent pay and our house on Ridge Road is paid off. Linda's a nurse at the district hospital, our two are grown, Marisol teaches and Danny's an electrician. But I've watched the north pit go driverless three years back, forty-odd trucks running themselves with nobody in the cab. So I don't trust the company's smile, put it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so, it was oversold like everything else they sell us. At the crib table I'd be the one grinning about it. Online, I don't do online, Linda does the internet in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AI Plateau means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means I finish my time in the cab and walk out at sixty-five with my pension. The AI stuff on the computers never touched me anyway, I don't even use the phone thing that writes your messages. It's the robot trucks I worry about, and those were coming whether this was hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, I'd keep driving and keep paying into the pension fund. Maybe go to one more union meeting a year, because the trucks are a separate fight. I'd probably finally fix the back deck I keep promising Linda.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. Like a storm that turned around before it reached the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the north pit going driverless. Does that change how you'd hear AI Plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. Hype or no hype, the trucks in the north pit don't need anyone smart, they just need GPS and a company that wants to save wages. So even in this picture I'd keep one eye on the union noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing much changes, what does the next few years look like for you and Linda?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seven more years of loops, then out. Linda wants to drive the coast road for a month and I've said yes. The plan's already made, this picture just lets us keep it.

S0.say: I'd tell the crib table it was all oversold, like I always said. I wouldn't post anything because Linda handles the internet in our house.
S0.think: Privately he thinks this lets him finish his time in the cab and retire at sixty-five with his pension. The thinking AI never touched him; the driverless trucks are the real worry either way.
S0.do: Keeps driving and paying into his retirement fund with no change. Goes to one or two more union meetings a year to keep an eye on automation of the trucks.
S0.feel: Relief, like a storm turning away before it reached the house, with a small watchful worry about the trucks.
S0.quote: Like a storm that turned around before it reached the house.
S0.fieldNote: Sam separates thinking AI from robots very clearly; the driverless trucks at the north pit are already real to him. His security comes from a paid-off house and a union job, and he doesn't use any AI tools. Even in the mildest picture he keeps an eye on the union noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to get in front of this now, not after. I'd be saying it at the meeting and at the pub, that the company will take every task it can and call it progress. People would know where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think Steady Disruption means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I think I squeak through. Seven years is short, and they'll automate the young guys' jobs on the new pit before they bother retraining an old haul driver. But I'd be angry about it, because that's not how it should go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for the union's technology committee, the one nobody wants to sit on. I'd push Linda and me to put an extra few hundred a month aside, just so we've got room if they offer a package. And I'd keep driving, I'm not going anywhere till they make me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit sour. Not scared for myself, more like watching a tide come in on other people's cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rudy's nephew Kev, he's twenty-six and drives the water cart, two kids. Jobs like his are the first the company would hand to a machine. I'd worry about the young ones with mortgages, not the old ones like me with the house paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust the company's smile. What would you want the union to win in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Any job that goes to a machine, the person gets first pick of the new jobs, paid training on company time, and no forced redundancies before fifty-five. And a share of what they save, because the savings come off our backs. I know they'd fight us on that last one.

S1.say: I'd tell the meeting and the pub that the union has to get in front of this now, before the company takes every task and calls it progress. People would know where I stand.
S1.think: He thinks he'll likely squeak through to retirement because they'll automate younger workers' jobs first. That makes him angry rather than relieved, because it isn't fair to the young ones.
S1.do: Joins the union's technology committee and pushes for first pick of new jobs, paid training and no forced redundancies before fifty-five. Puts a few hundred extra a month aside in case a package is offered, and keeps driving.
S1.feel: Uneasy and a bit sour, not scared for himself but troubled for younger workers with mortgages.
S1.quote: Not scared for myself, more like watching a tide come in on other people's cars.
S1.fieldNote: His worry points outward, at young workers like Rudy's nephew Kev, not at himself. He blames the company for taking savings off workers' backs and turns straight to the union. Resistant to new tools, he plans to protect what exists rather than learn anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace that they let it happen with no plan for working people. I'd be at the gate if the union called a stop-work, and I'd say so loudly. Two years is nothing, the government wouldn't even have its forms printed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2028 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means the truck goes driverless and so do I, at sixty, five years short. I'd be all right money-wise, I think, we've got about a year and a half of living put away and the house is ours. But I'd be the guy at home at sixty with nothing to get up for, and that scares me more than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Linda and the bank the first week and work out the bridge to the pension. Cut the second car and the fishing trip, get the union fighting for a proper redundancy, and write to our member of parliament, which I've never done in my life. If they offer a package early I'd take it rather than wait to be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Like the floor's been pulled out and you're still standing there wondering why your feet feel funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be about sixty when this arrives. What does that gap to your pension look like in real numbers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eighteen months of savings, plus Linda's wage if she keeps going, plus whatever redundancy the union squeezes out. That gets us to sixty-five if we're careful, no new car, no coast trip. Linda would have to work longer than she planned, and I'd hate asking her that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't much warning. What would you do in the first month after you heard it was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring my union delegate, then sit Danny down, because his electrician work could go too with the robots. I'd want to tell him before he hears it on the news. And I'd tell Linda to keep her job, which is a strange thing to say to your wife when you're the one who always wanted her to slow down.

S2.say: I'd say loudly that it's a disgrace to let this happen with no plan for working people, and I'd be at the gate if the union called a stop-work. Two years is nothing.
S2.think: He believes his truck goes driverless and so does he, at sixty, five years short of his pension. The money would probably stretch, but being at home with nothing to get up for scares him more.
S2.do: Works out a bridge to his pension with Linda and the bank in the first week, cuts the second car and the fishing trip, and pushes the union for proper redundancy. Writes to his member of parliament and would take an early package rather than wait to be pushed.
S2.feel: Gutted and unsteady, more afraid of losing his purpose than his income, and uncomfortable asking Linda to work longer.
S2.quote: I'd be the guy at home at sixty with nothing to get up for, and that scares me more than the money.
S2.fieldNote: With two years' warning his cushion holds but his sense of purpose doesn't. He reaches for the union and, for the first time, politics. The strangest moment for him is asking Linda to keep working after years of wanting her to slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but I'd say we've got time to fight, so let's fight properly. I'd be telling the young ones to join the union now, not when the letter comes. I'd be the boring old guy at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2031 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three. That's close enough that I could probably hang on, or take a package and call it retirement, two years early is not the end of the world. It's the young ones it would hit, again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and put every spare bit into the pension fund, a proper push. I'd stay on the technology committee and fight for a deal on transfers and retraining. And I'd plan for leaving at sixty-two or sixty-three on my terms, not theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe in this one. Like with the slow one, it's a fight I'd get to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different for you from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a shock, five years is a plan. In five I'd have the bridge saved properly and Linda could still cut her shifts. In two I'm just reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in those five years that you couldn't do in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fight for the deal at the table, not at the gate. I'd want the union to have a signed agreement before the first robot truck turns up in our pit. In two years you're grabbing what you can, in five you can actually negotiate.

S3.say: I'd say we've got time to fight, so let's fight properly, and tell the young ones to join the union now rather than when the letter comes.
S3.think: At sixty-three he could hang on or take a package and call it retirement, and two years early is not the end of the world. He sees the real damage landing on younger workers again.
S3.do: Keeps driving while putting every spare dollar into his retirement fund. Stays on the union technology committee to win a signed deal on transfers and retraining, and plans to leave at sixty-two or sixty-three on his own terms.
S3.feel: Uneasy but able to breathe, because it feels like a fight he'd get to finish.
S3.quote: Two years is a shock, five years is a plan.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn panic-buying into negotiating for him. He talks about a signed agreement before the first robot truck arrives, which is more strategic than the fast picture. His own landing looks soft; his energy goes into the fight for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time enough for the government to do it right, so no excuses. Training, pensions, a share of the profits for towns like ours. If they botch it with ten years' notice, that's on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2036 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it doesn't, I'm out by sixty-five with the truck still needing me, most likely. I'll be on the back deck by the time the robots come. It's my kids' world it changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much at work, I'd drive to sixty-five as planned. I'd keep up the union stuff, and I'd sit with the kids about their plans, Danny especially. Maybe help him with a course if he wants to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about me, uneasy for them. It's an odd feeling, being safe while you watch your kids' ground shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: By 2036 you'd be sixty-eight. Does this one touch you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly, I'll be gone from the pit. But I'd feel it every time I drove past the gate and saw nobody in the cabs. Nineteen years, then twenty-six, and it'd be like we never sat there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marisol and Danny in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Danny that electricians wire up the robots before the robots wire up anything, so get on the right side of that. And I'd tell Marisol to stay teaching, kids still need a person in the room. I'd help with money for a course, we've got enough for that.

S4.say: I'd say a decade is plenty of time for the government to do it right, with training, pensions and a share of the profits for mining towns. If they botch it with ten years' notice, that's on them.
S4.think: He expects to be retired on the back deck before the robots reach his pit, so it barely touches him. It's his children's world that changes.
S4.do: Drives to sixty-five as planned and keeps up his union work. Sits down with his children about their plans and offers to pay for a course if Danny wants to switch.
S4.feel: Calm about himself but uneasy for his kids, an odd mix of being safe while their ground shifts.
S4.quote: It's an odd feeling, being safe while you watch your kids' ground shift.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years puts Sam past retirement, and he says so plainly. His concern moves fully to his children and to the empty cabs he'd see from the gate. He holds government to a higher standard when it has a decade's warning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is a proper bridge to the pension for anyone over fifty-five, paid for by the companies that save the wages, and the union having a seat at the table before the trucks arrive, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. If the pit goes driverless, the pub, the football club, the shops on Ridge Road all lose their customers. I'd be fine. The town wouldn't be.

headlineQuote: Nineteen years, then twenty-six, and it'd be like we never sat there.
portrait: Sam Torres is a 58-year-old haul truck driver at a large open-pit copper mine, a loyal union man with a paid-off house and a nurse for a partner. He has watched a nearby pit go driverless and distrusts the company, though he never uses AI tools himself. In the mild pictures he plans to drive to his pension and fight for younger workers through the union. The two-year AGI picture shakes him, less over money than over being at home at sixty with nothing to do. With five or ten years' warning he relaxes into planning, and his concern moves to his children and his town.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because the truck would go driverless and he would be out at sixty, five years short of his pension.
whatWouldHelp: A proper bridge to the pension for anyone over fifty-five, paid for by the companies that save the wages, and the union at the table before the trucks arrive.
